title: How to Prune and Reprice an AliDropship Catalog Each Quarter
excerpt: A dropshipping catalog grows by default and quietly eats attention and ad budget. Here is a quarterly pass to bucket, fix, reprice, and remove listings using rules you can reuse every cycle.
body: A dropshipping catalog grows by default. Every research session adds products, few sessions remove any, and after two quarters you are spreading attention, apps, and ad budget across hundreds of listings that produce almost nothing. AliDropship makes importing and automating easy, which is exactly why a scheduled pruning pass matters. The goal is not a smaller catalog for its own sake but a catalog where every live product justifies the attention it consumes.

Run the pass on a fixed calendar rather than when you feel like it, and once a quarter is enough for most stores. Pull a single sheet with every active product, its total orders, its page views, its ad spend if any, and its current landed margin. Four columns decide the fate of everything: demand, traffic, spend, and profit. Products with neither demand nor traffic after a full quarter are not going to suddenly work, and keeping them live only dilutes your collections and your internal search.

Sort the list into three buckets. Keep: products with consistent orders and a margin above your floor. Fix: products with traffic but weak conversion, or orders but thin margin. Remove: products with no orders and no meaningful traffic, plus anything whose margin has fallen below the floor and cannot be repriced without going uncompetitive. Most stores find roughly a fifth of the catalog lands in the remove bucket on the first pass, and that number shrinks each cycle as your sourcing improves.

Handle the fix bucket one change at a time. If a product gets traffic but does not convert, the cause is usually the page rather than the product: weak images, a title that does not match how shoppers search, or a shipping estimate buried below the fold. Change one element, give it two weeks, then check again. If a product converts but earns too little, test a price increase before cutting it, because a price ten percent higher often loses fewer sales than it gains in margin.

Repricing deserves its own rule. Do not reprice one product in isolation. Group products by landed cost band and move the whole band together, so the catalog never develops strange gaps where a larger size costs less than a smaller one. Recompute the floor after every supplier cost change, and check that any holiday discount you plan still clears it. A promotion that pushes a best seller below its floor is the fastest way to post record revenue in a month with nothing left over.

Finish by recording what you removed and why. A short note each cycle on which categories failed and which suppliers produced the keepers turns the pruning pass into sourcing intelligence. After two or three cycles the patterns are obvious: a category that never converts, a supplier whose costs drift every quarter, a price band that always wins. Act on those patterns at import time and the catalog stops needing rescuing. The DTCwise Dropshipping category at /category/dropshipping keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, and the AliDropship page at /tool/alidropship covers how its automation and catalog tools support this routine.
